notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 map a sharp C4/C5 root split and inspect costs/purities; step 2 recover high-value C5+ products with a small tree; step 3 add light-end separation only if profitable; step 4 tune stages/reflux and prune weak columns.
Feed has most value in C5+; blends offer cheaper recovery where pure separation is difficult. Initial column targets C4/C5 at moderate severity to learn split and annual cost.

note: Build a blend-oriented backbone with sharp volatility cuts: C3/C4 lights, C5 blend, and C6 paraffin blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish sharp C4/C5 root and blend-yielding C3/C4, C5/C6+ cuts; step 2 recover high-value C6 and heavy products; step 3 add pure separations only where incremental value pays; step 4 tune/prune.
Root at 55/3.5 was too diffuse and cost $221M. Use sharper 70/4.5 and lower pressure. C4 and C5 blends retain ~85-90% of pure value with much easier separations. Initial 4-column tree tests saleable C3/C4/C5/C6-paraffin products and cost scale.

note: Rebalance the root to move C5 overhead, sharpen the C4/C5 split, and test saleable C5 and C6-paraffin blends with a cheaper three-column backbone.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a C4/C5 root and sharp C4/C5 split so the C5 blend sells; step 2 make C6 paraffin blend from root bottoms; step 3 add pure/heavy separations only if incremental value pays; step 4 tune/prune.
Current root 70/4.5/4.5 is expensive and leaves half the N-pentane in B, contaminating the C6 blend. T at 45/2.5/3 leaves 32% butane in C5. Increase root boil-up to move C5 overhead, while lowering stages/reflux/pressure to control cost. Make T a sharper C4/C5 column and simplify B to C6-paraffin vs heavies. Remove premature BB. Target C5 revenue ~$171M and C6-paraffin ~$300M.

note: Make a clean C5/C6 root cut, then isolate the C5 blend with a sharper C4/C5 split; defer the unsold heavy branch.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a C5/C6 root and sharp C4/C5 split so the C5 blend sells; step 2 make C6 paraffin blend from root bottoms; step 3 add pure/heavy separations only if incremental value pays; step 4 tune/prune.
Prior root at 50/3/5 took DMB overhead and cost $289M. Reduce boil-up and stages to put the C5/C6 cut near 1395 mol/s tops. T must now deliver ~695 mol/s of 95% C5 blend; use 55 stages and R5. Sell B temporarily to isolate whether this backbone can generate revenue before adding the C6 branch. Higher pressure drop should reduce cold-condenser cost.

note: Adopt the profitable root/C6-paraffin backbone and split its clean light tops at C4/C5 to unlock the valuable C5 blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 adopt the proven clean C5/C6 root and C6-paraffin branch; step 2 split root tops into saleable C4/C5 then C3/C4 blends; step 3 recover heavy products only where value exceeds cost; step 4 tune expensive columns.
R170 earns 0.728 with root 65/5/6/dp.35 sending essentially all C5 and lighter overhead, and B 80/7/5/dp.3 producing a clean 790 mol/s C6-paraffin blend. Its 1562 mol/s T is almost exactly C3+C4+C5, so a single sharp C4/C5 column should unlock about $609M/yr C5 revenue. Copy it and test T at 60 stages, R5, boil-up 4; preserve the proven root and B settings.

note: Sharpen both light-end splits enough to meet the 95% blend specifications; the prior moderate columns left large amounts of butane in C5 and C3 in C4.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 retain the proven clean C5/C6 root and C6-paraffin branch; step 2 make genuinely saleable C5 and C4 blends with sharper splitters; step 3 recover heavy products only where value exceeds cost; step 4 tune expensive columns.
The first T splitter was much too weak: TB remained only 77% C5 with 22% n-butane. R214 also shows that a 45-stage C3/C4 splitter leaves C4 at only 90%. Increase T to 100 stages, R8/boil7 to drive butane overhead while retaining pentanes, and use TT 60/R5/boil6 to target >95% C4. C5 revenue is about $619M/yr, so this substantial separation duty can pay. Preserve root and B unchanged.

note: Restore the island's best validated four-column design: moderate C4/C5 separation achieves the C5 blend and 96% n-butane at much lower cost than my oversized columns.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 retain the proven clean C5/C6 root and C6-paraffin branch; step 2 make saleable C5 and C4 blends with the validated 55/5/7 and 45/4/5 splitters; step 3 recover heavy products only where value exceeds cost; step 4 tune expensive columns. Copy R262: its moderate 55-stage T column gives clean C5 bottoms, while its 45-stage TT column sells 96% n-butane. This yields $1712M revenue and reward 1.982, much better than my overly tall, costly splitters. Next, investigate whether the light tops can produce C3 mix economically, then consider heavy-branch separation.

note: Reduce the expensive C6-paraffin splitter's stages and reflux while preserving its boil-up, using the existing purity margin to cut cost.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 retain the proven clean C5/C6 root and C6-paraffin branch; step 2 make saleable C5 and C4 blends with validated splitters; step 3 recover heavy products only where value exceeds cost; step 4 tune expensive columns. Current best R262 gives reward 1.982. Heavy and light extra columns were unprofitable in R311/R309. I am now reducing the costly 80/7 C6-paraffin splitter to 70/6 while keeping boil-up 5; its overhead is about 98% C6 paraffin, so there is some purity margin. If this retains the $942M blend, continue cost tuning; otherwise revert.

note: Continue the successful heavy-splitter cost reduction: 70/6 improved both revenue and cost, so test 60/5 while retaining boil-up 5 and watch the 95% C6 blend limit.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 retain the proven clean C5/C6 root and C6-paraffin branch; step 2 preserve saleable C5 and n-butane; step 3 defer heavy/light recovery because prior trains lost money; step 4 tune costly columns. Best is 2.151 with four columns. Reducing B from 80/7 to 70/6 both cut cost and raised C6 blend revenue to $1001.7M, so test 60/5 at unchanged boil-up 5. More C6 paraffin overhead is beneficial while total non-blend naphthenes must stay below 5%. Root 65/5 costs $373M and T $169M, so they are the next major targets. TT at 45/4 costs only $52M and is lower priority.

note: Adopt the island-best heavy-recovery train and test whether a modest upgrade of the inexpensive n-butane column reaches the 99% premium threshold.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R402's validated 2.269 seven-column plant; step 2 seek low-cost purity upgrades and trim major columns; step 3 retain only changes that improve reward. The heavy train adds about $52M/yr net by selling 99% octane. B=60/5 destroyed the C6 blend, so retain B=70/6. First test a modest TT upgrade (45/4 to 50/5): TTB is already 96% n-butane, and reaching 99% would add about $30M/yr premium revenue for a small-column cost increase. Root and T remain expensive but prior root reduction caused severe purity losses.

note: Adopt the best heavy train and increase only the octane column's reflux, targeting the 99% premium threshold without changing the validated cuts.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R453's validated 2.603 plant; step 2 optimize the small heavy columns for premium purity; step 3 test major-column cost reductions only where purity margin allows. R453's BBB=60/8/3 gives 99% heptane worth $223M/yr, while BBBB=60/8/7 gives 98% octane worth $207M. Its TT=45/4 is better than my 50/5 (slightly more net profit). First copy R453 and raise only BBBB reflux to 10: reaching 99% octane should add about $40M/yr revenue for a modest small-column cost increase. Root=65/5/6, B=70/6/5 and T=55/5/7 must remain fixed: earlier root/B reductions destroyed valuable blend purity.

note: Adopt the best heavy train and test slightly stronger octane stripping: boil-up 15 still leaves substantial octane in the bottoms, so 18 may add premium octane profitably.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R505's validated 2.730 heavy-recovery train; step 2 optimize final octane stripping; step 3 consider only high-value residual recovery or low-risk cost trims. R505's BBBB=60/8/15 recovers 193 mol/s octane at 99% for $292.5M/yr; versus boil-up 12 it gains $24.4M revenue for $8.6M cost. Test boil-up 18 to recover some of the remaining ~44 mol/s octane in its nonane-rich bottoms. Keep root=65/5/6, B=70/6/5, T=55/5/7, TT=45/4/5, BB=50/3.5/4.5 and BBB=60/8/3 fixed: these jointly deliver C5/C6 blends, 96% butane and premium heptane. R501's extra BBT columns failed to sell anything and are not worth copying.

note: Copy the profitable nonane polisher, then increase its rectification to target saleable octane overhead in addition to pure nonane bottoms.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R554's validated 2.897 nonane-recovery train; step 2 upgrade its small final splitter to recover saleable octane overhead as well as nonane bottoms; step 3 tune only this polisher, then consider low-risk cost trims. R554 uses BBBB=60/8/15 and BBBBB=45/4/6: bottoms are 46 mol/s 100% nonane ($92.7M), but 59 mol/s tops at 73% octane are unsold. Since this final feed is only C8/C9 and the volatility gap is wide, 60 stages/reflux 8 at the same boil-up 6 should sharpen the overhead toward 95–99% octane without sacrificing nonane. Avoid R550 boil-up 8, which reduced nonane recovery. Keep every proven upstream setting fixed.

note: Combine R598’s cheaper, higher-recovery octane column with my strong nonane polisher; this should retain both products while saving substantial reflux cost.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 retain the validated 3.102 backbone and strong 60/8/6 nonane polisher; step 2 reduce BBBB reflux from 8 to 4, which R598 proved saves $34.5M and recovers 36 mol/s more 99% octane; step 3 let the strong polisher monetize the resulting C8/C9 bottoms, then trim other proven-margin columns. Current polisher converts 106 mol/s 59% nonane feed into 45 mol/s 97% octane plus 61 mol/s pure nonane, worth $188.9M for only $25.9M. R598's weaker final column wasted its tops, but that does not indict its superior upstream split. With BBBB=60/4/15 its bottoms are 69 mol/s 90% nonane; 60/8/6 should produce clean nonane bottoms and potentially saleable octane tops. Keep all other settings fixed.

note: Adopt the island-best validated design: its naphthene branch is net profitable, and its smaller C4/C5 splitter saves cost while retaining both saleable products.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R649’s validated 3.219 plant, which combines the cheaper C4/C5 splitter, higher-recovery octane stripper, strong nonane polisher, and a profitable naphthene branch. Step 2 optimize the new BBT/BBTB train: its unsold BBTBT and BBTBB streams still contain valuable material, but added separation must beat column cost. Step 3 trim large proven-margin columns, especially root and B, only after securing the improved baseline. R649 gains $155.1M naphthene revenue for $114.7M added column cost and saves $26.2M at T versus my current design. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15 and BBBBB=60/8/6; these jointly recover 229 mol/s 99% octane and 41 mol/s pure nonane.

note: Add a dedicated cyclohexane/heptane splitter on the unsold BBTBB stream; unlike strengthening BBTB, this directly targets both product purities without sacrificing the existing naphthene overhead.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 preserve R649’s validated 3.219 plant. Step 2 recover valuable unsold streams where a small column can beat its cost: first split BBTBB (118 mol/s, 73% heptane) into saleable heptane bottoms and potentially naphthene tops; stronger BBTB itself was proven counterproductive by R695. Step 3 optimize the cheap nonane polisher for higher total nonane recovery, then trim large columns only with clear purity margin. Current core economics: revenue $2573.9M, cost $1162.4M. Naphthene train adds $155.1M for $114.7M. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15 and BBBBB=60/8/6 pending tests. TTT C3 splitting failed in R694: added $44.3M cost and no saleable product.

note: Finish the remaining cyclohexane/heptane binary cut: both outlets have plausible saleable value, and this small stream should need only a low-cost column.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 preserve the validated 3.443 plant. Step 2 finish the residual cyclohexane/heptane cut BBTBBT (56 mol/s, 57/43): a small binary splitter should recover both saleable products for much less than their ~$90M/yr combined value. Step 3 strengthen only the nonane polisher to try to sell its octane-rich overhead while retaining premium nonane bottoms. Current base: revenue $2695.2M, cost $1185.3M. BBTBB=60/6/6 beats R740’s 60/8/10 (more heptane, lower cost). TTT C3 splitting and BBTT C6 splitting have both failed economically; backbone trimming destroyed C6 purity. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15.

note: Target the two remaining nearly saleable small binary cuts with more rectification and stages; both use inexpensive columns and avoid the failed high-boil-up nonane approach.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 preserve the validated 3.544 plant. Step 2 finish the two remaining small binary streams: strengthen BBTBBT so its 82%-heptane bottoms reach 95%, and strengthen BBBBB so its 77%-nonane overhead reaches 95% while retaining premium bottoms. Step 3 if these work, trim their duties; if not, stop adding columns and test only high-value local settings. Current base revenue $2750.4M, cost $1196.2M. BBTBB=60/6/6 beats milder alternatives. TTT C3 and BBTT C6 splitting failed economically; backbone trimming destroyed C6 purity. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15. Nonane boil-up 10 was harmful (R792), so target nonane via reflux/stages instead.

note: Combine the island-best cyclohexane recovery with my higher-recovery nonane polisher, and push the nearly saleable 93% heptane bottoms over 95% using a modest increase in stages and duties.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 adopt R838 (3.550), whose cyclohexane finisher is best. Step 2 combine it with my proven 80/15/6 nonane polisher and strengthen BBTBBT just enough to make its 93%-heptane bottoms saleable. Step 3 trim or fine-tune only the small finishers; preserve the profitable backbone. R838 BBTBBT=60/8/10 gives premium cyclohexane and 93% heptane, so 70/10/12 should cross 95%. R838 nonane=60/8/6 saves cost but loses 9 mol/s nonane versus my 80/15/6; restoring it should add about $14M net. TTT C3 and BBTT C6 splits failed economically; backbone trimming destroyed C6 purity. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15 and BBTBB=60/6/6.

note: Interpolate the tiny binary finisher between the two observed extremes and adopt the proven cheaper upstream column; this targets saleable heptane bottoms without sacrificing the premium cyclohexane tops.
notebook: PLAN: Preserve the validated backbone and high-recovery nonane polisher. Use the remaining solves to (1) combine R887's cheaper 45/5/5 BBTBB with an intermediate 60/8/11 finisher, aiming to retain pure cyclohexane overhead while lifting its 93% heptane bottoms over 95%; (2) if needed, bracket boil-up around 11 or revert. Current best 3.573. R885 showed 8/15 makes heptane pure but cyclohexane only 90%, while 8/10 gives pure cyclohexane and 93% heptane, so 11 is the most promising interpolation. TTT and BBTT recovery proved uneconomic; do not disturb the main splitters.

note: Target the largest remaining premium upgrade: TTB is already 95% n-butane, so stronger rectification may reach 99% and add about $30M/yr while leaving all saleable heavy products unchanged.
notebook: PLAN: Preserve the 3.682 backbone. With 9 solves left, first test a stronger TT splitter for 99% premium n-butane (potential +$30M/yr revenue); if the gain does not cover its extra cost, revert and instead trim the nonane polisher or tiny binary finisher. TTT and BBTT recovery were previously uneconomic; avoid major topology changes. Current finisher 60/8/11 already sells both outlets, and 70/10/13 is not better.

note: Restore the best design and test the remaining potentially valuable cut: BBTT contains separate C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blend pools, so one sharp column could make both outlets saleable.
notebook: PLAN: Restore the 3.682 backbone, then use the remaining solves on the largest recoverable unsold stream. Step 1: test one rigorous BBTT paraffin/naphthene splitter at 80/8/8; both outlets can qualify as blends, giving up to about $100M/yr revenue. If uneconomic, revert and make only low-risk cost trims. Best backbone uses TT 45/4/5, BBTBB 45/5/5, finisher 60/8/11. Stronger TT 60/6/5 loses money despite more C4 recovery.

note: Restore the best design and sharpen the BBTT paraffin/naphthene split substantially; the weak 80-stage trial established the direction but neither outlet met blend purity.
notebook: PLAN: Restore the 3.682 backbone and make a final rigorous attempt to monetize BBTT, the largest unsold heavy stream. The 80/8/8 split was too weak (87% paraffin overhead, 70% naphthene bottoms), so test 120/15/15: both outlets can be blends worth about $217M/yr combined. If uneconomic, revert and finish. Proven best: TT 45/4/5, BBTBB 45/5/5, finisher 60/8/11, nonane polisher 80/15/6.

note: The strong BBTT split leaves its overhead only 1% below the saleable C6-paraffin blend threshold. Extra rectification should monetize that overhead without requiring the naphthene bottoms to reach specification.
notebook: PLAN: Use the remaining solves only on the terminal BBTT splitter, since upstream changes would exhaust the budget re-solving the whole train. At 120/15/15 its overhead is 94% C6 paraffin, just below the 95% blend threshold worth about $141M/yr. Increase reflux to 18 while holding boil-up at 15 to cross that threshold; bottoms need not sell for this to beat the 3.682 base if added net value exceeds column cost. Best backbone: TT 45/4/5, BBTBB 45/5/5, finisher 60/8/11, nonane polisher 80/15/6; BBTT is otherwise sold. Prior 80/8/8 and 120/15/15 trials failed to monetize either outlet.

note: The current BBTT overhead sells, but 26% n-hexane contamination keeps its valuable naphthene bottoms off-spec. A taller, higher-reflux terminal split targets both blend products without disturbing any upstream column.
notebook: PLAN: Spend the last five solves solely on BBTT, the only terminal change with large upside. The 120/18/15 column monetizes its overhead ($131M/yr) but its bottoms remain 74% C6 naphthene, leaving about $147M/yr unsold. Test 160/25/20 to drive nearly all n-hexane overhead while retaining the saleable paraffin cut. If close, strengthen rectification further; if not, retain the 3.739 design. Backbone and all other terminal settings are proven and must remain unchanged to conserve solves.

note: Use the maximum practical rectification and stage count for the difficult n-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut; recovering the naphthene blend is worth far more than the incremental column cost if the paraffin overhead remains on-spec.
notebook: PLAN: Use the remaining four solves only on BBTT. At 160/25/20 its paraffin overhead sells ($133M/yr), but 34 mol/s n-hexane remains in the 137 mol/s bottoms, leaving the $151M/yr naphthene blend off-spec. Make one maximum-separation test at 200/30/30: the required target is roughly 145 mol/s overhead and 103 mol/s nearly pure naphthene bottoms. If this succeeds or comes close, retain/tune it; otherwise revert to the validated 3.739 design. Do not alter the proven backbone or other terminal columns.

note: Maximum stages and reflux at moderate pressure still leave the naphthene bottoms off-spec. Try much lower column pressure to improve the very close n-hexane/methylcyclopentane relative volatility; the validated best design remains available by revert.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the validated 3.739 design and use the last three solves only on the difficult BBTT hexane/naphthene separation. Maximum stages/reflux at dp=0.2 still leaves 16% hexane in the bottoms. Test the same maximum separation at dp=0.9: much lower pressure may increase relative volatility enough to reach 95% naphthene while retaining the saleable paraffin overhead. If unsuccessful, revert to 3.739; do not alter the proven backbone.
At 200/30/30/0.2, BBTT costs $194.7M/yr and overhead sells for $151.1M/yr, but its 123 mol/s bottoms are only 84% naphthene. The potential extra blend revenue is about $152M/yr. Earlier 160/25/20 was the best net setting (3.739). Other terminal polishers are not worth further changes.

note: Keep the successful low-pressure BBTT split but reduce stages and reflux to the previously best net setting; this should cut cost while preserving the saleable paraffin overhead.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the 3.863 low-pressure BBTT design and spend the final two solves reducing that column's cost while retaining its saleable C6-paraffin overhead. First test the previously best-performing 160/25/20 separation at dp=0.9; if the overhead stays on-spec, this should preserve revenue and save capital/energy versus 200/30/30. If it fails, revert. Do not alter the proven backbone.
At 200/30/30/0.9, BBTT costs only $70.3M/yr versus $194.7M/yr at dp=0.2, and its overhead sells for $149.7M/yr; bottoms remain an unsellable 83% naphthene. Low pressure gave the large reward gain through cost, not bottoms purity. Earlier 160/25/20 at moderate pressure was the best net BBTT setting. Other terminal polishers and TTT recovery are not worth risking the remaining solves.

note: Use the final solve for a low-risk cost trim: BBTT's overhead is about 98% C6 paraffins, so 140 stages should retain the saleable blend while reducing column cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Final solve: retain the proven 3.866 backbone and trim only BBTT from 160 to 140 stages at 25/20/dp0.9. Its overhead is comfortably above the 95% C6-paraffin blend threshold (about 98%), so modest stage reduction may preserve all revenue while lowering capital. Best valid design remains protected if this fails.
BBTT at 200/30/30/0.9 costs $70.3M/yr; 160/25/20/0.9 costs $51.9M/yr and retains the $132.5M/yr overhead. Bottoms remain unsellable even under extreme separation. Other tested changes (TTB premium upgrade, BBTT naphthene recovery, terminal polishers) did not improve net reward. No further solves remain after this trial.
